quotes.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
quotes.context: Said at his trial in Athens in 399 BCE, when he chose death over giving up philosophy. It is the founding line for the idea that questioning your own beliefs is part of living well.

quotes.text: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.
quotes.context: The opening of a book asking what could make political authority legitimate. It inspired revolutionaries in France and still frames debates about freedom and society.

quotes.text: The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it.
quotes.context: A short note, published after his death, that became the motto of a politics focused on action. It is engraved on his grave in Highgate Cemetery in London.

quotes.text: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
quotes.who: Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949)
quotes.context: The key line of a founding text of modern feminism. Her argument was that much of what society calls 'feminine' is learned rather than natural.

quotes.text: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs.
quotes.context: A classic statement of liberal freedom. Mill's 'harm principle' says society should only restrict what you do when it harms others.

quotes.text: Society is indeed a contract... a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.
quotes.who: Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)
quotes.context: Burke was writing against the French Revolution's attempt to rebuild society from scratch. It is a founding statement of conservatism: we inherit institutions and owe a duty to pass them on.

quotes.text: Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.
quotes.who: Martin Luther King Jr, Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963)
quotes.context: Written in jail in reply to white clergymen who called his protests 'unwise and untimely'. He argued that no one can stand aside from injustice in another place.

quotes.text: The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house.
quotes.context: Said at a feminist conference where she criticised the absence of Black and lesbian women. She argued that a movement which copies the exclusions it opposes cannot bring real change.

quotes.text: Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.
quotes.context: From an essay on the duty of writers to tell the truth about their society. Baldwin is a guide to looking honestly at hard things without losing hope.

quotes.text: If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.
quotes.who: George Orwell, 'The Freedom of the Press' (1945)
quotes.context: Written as a preface for Animal Farm, which publishers were nervous about because it criticised the Soviet Union, then a wartime ally. The preface itself was not published until 1972.

quotes.text: The curious task of economics is to demonstrate to men how little they really know about what they imagine they can design.
quotes.context: Hayek argued that no planner can know enough to run an economy, and that markets pass on knowledge that is spread across millions of people. It is a key idea for free-market thinkers.

quotes.text: There is no such thing as society. There are individual men and women and there are families.
quotes.who: Margaret Thatcher, interview in Woman's Own (1987)
quotes.context: Often quoted as a dismissal of community. In context she went on to say people must look after themselves and then their neighbours. It is a good example of how a quote can be used to mean different things.

quotes.text: Democracy is the worst form of Government except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.
quotes.context: Churchill introduced it as something that 'has been said', so he was quoting a view rather than claiming it as his own. It is a classic defence of democracy as imperfect but better than the alternatives.

quotes.text: I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities.
quotes.context: From his speech from the dock, facing a possible death sentence. He ended by saying it was an ideal for which he was prepared to die. He then spent 27 years in prison.

quotes.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
quotes.who: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776)
quotes.context: Smith's point was that trade can serve everyone even when each person acts for themselves. He also wrote a whole book on sympathy and morality, so he was not simply praising selfishness.

quotes.text: The single story creates stereotypes, and the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete.
quotes.context: From her talk 'The Danger of a Single Story', about how people and places get reduced to one narrative. One of the most watched TED talks.

quotes.text: Freedom for the pike is death for the minnows.
quotes.who: Isaiah Berlin, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958)
quotes.context: Berlin was explaining why total freedom for the strong can leave the weak with none. He distinguished 'negative' liberty, being left alone, from 'positive' liberty, being able to act.

quotes.text: To be conservative, then, is to prefer the familiar to the unknown, to prefer the tried to the untried, fact to mystery, the actual to the possible.
quotes.context: Oakeshott described conservatism as a temperament rather than a fixed programme. It is a thoughtful case for caution about big plans.

quotes.text: Feminism is a movement to end sexism, sexist exploitation, and oppression.
quotes.who: bell hooks, Feminism Is for Everybody (2000)
quotes.context: hooks wanted a definition that did not set women against men. By targeting sexism rather than men, she argued, feminism could include everyone.

quotes.text: In nature nothing exists alone.
quotes.context: Carson showed how pesticides moved through food chains and harmed wildlife. Her book helped launch the modern environmental movement.

quotes.text: Until the lions have their own historians, the history of the hunt will always glorify the hunter.
quotes.who: African proverb, popularised by Chinua Achebe
quotes.context: Achebe used it to explain why he wrote Things Fall Apart: to tell the story of colonialism from the African side. It is a reminder to ask who is telling the story.

ideologies.name: Liberalism
ideologies.oneLine: Individual freedom, protected by law and limited government.
ideologies.believes: Each person has rights that the state must respect: free speech, religion, property, a fair trial. Government should rest on consent and be limited by a constitution. In modern usage it splits between classical liberals, who stress free markets, and social liberals, who think the state should help people have real opportunities.
ideologies.origins: Grew out of the Enlightenment and the reaction to absolute monarchy and religious wars, with thinkers like John Locke in the 1600s, and later Adam Smith and John Stuart Mill.
ideologies.critics: Conservatives say it dissolves the traditions, families and communities that make freedom meaningful. Socialists say formal rights mean little without economic equality. Communitarians argue it treats people as isolated individuals when we are shaped by our relationships.
ideologies.thinkers: John Locke, John Stuart Mill, John Rawls, Isaiah Berlin

ideologies.name: Conservatism
ideologies.oneLine: Caution about rapid change, and respect for tradition and institutions.
ideologies.believes: Society is complex and has grown over time, so tested institutions like family, religion, the law and the nation carry wisdom that is easy to lose. Change should be gradual and practical rather than driven by abstract theories. Many conservatives also value order, duty and personal responsibility.
ideologies.origins: Edmund Burke's reaction to the French Revolution in 1790 is usually seen as the starting point. In Britain it developed through the Tory tradition, including Disraeli's 'one nation' conservatism.
ideologies.critics: Liberals and progressives say it can defend unfair hierarchies just because they are old. Critics on the left argue that 'tradition' often protects the powerful. Some free-market thinkers say it is too ready to use the state to enforce values.
ideologies.thinkers: Edmund Burke, Michael Oakeshott, Roger Scruton, Benjamin Disraeli

ideologies.name: Socialism
ideologies.oneLine: The economy should serve everyone, through shared or democratic ownership.
ideologies.believes: Capitalism creates deep inequality because owners profit from workers' labour. Key industries and resources should be owned or controlled collectively, whether by the state, by workers or by co-operatives. Equality and solidarity matter as much as individual freedom.
ideologies.origins: Arose in the early 1800s in response to the hardships of the Industrial Revolution. Early thinkers included Robert Owen; Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels later gave it a more revolutionary theory.
ideologies.critics: Free-market economists argue that central planning fails because no planner has enough information, as Hayek put it. Liberals worry that concentrating economic power in the state threatens freedom. Critics point to the economic failures and repression of states that called themselves socialist.
ideologies.thinkers: Robert Owen, Karl Marx, Rosa Luxemburg, R. H. Tawney

ideologies.name: Social democracy
ideologies.oneLine: Keep the market, but tame it with a strong welfare state.
ideologies.believes: Capitalism produces wealth but also insecurity, so the state should provide public services, social insurance and workers' rights. Change should come through elections, not revolution. Think of the NHS, or the Nordic model.
ideologies.origins: Developed from late nineteenth-century socialist parties that chose the democratic route. It shaped post-war Europe, including Britain's 1945 Labour government.
ideologies.critics: Free-market critics say high taxes and regulation slow growth and create dependence. Socialists say it only softens capitalism without changing who holds power. Others question whether it can survive globalisation and ageing populations.
ideologies.thinkers: Eduard Bernstein, Clement Attlee, Olof Palme, Anthony Crosland

ideologies.name: Libertarianism
ideologies.believes: People own themselves and should be free to do anything that does not harm others. Government should be limited to protecting rights, enforcing contracts and defence. Free markets and voluntary exchange are seen as both fair and efficient. Some go further and want no state at all.
ideologies.origins: Draws on classical liberalism, but became a distinct movement in twentieth-century America, influenced by economists of the Austrian school and the writer Ayn Rand.
ideologies.critics: Social liberals and socialists say it ignores how unequal starting points limit real freedom. Conservatives say it undervalues community and moral order. Others point to things markets do badly, like pollution or public health.
ideologies.thinkers: Robert Nozick, Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman, Ayn Rand

ideologies.name: Liberal feminism
ideologies.oneLine: Equal rights and opportunities for women within existing institutions.
ideologies.believes: Women are as capable as men and should have the same legal rights, education and access to work and public life. The focus is on reform through law: votes for women, equal pay, anti-discrimination rules.
ideologies.origins: Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), then the suffrage movements of the late 1800s and early 1900s.
ideologies.critics: Radical feminists say it tries to fit women into a system designed by men rather than changing it. Black and working-class feminists say it has often centred the concerns of middle-class white women. Conservatives argue it undervalues differences between men and women and the role of family.
ideologies.thinkers: Mary Wollstonecraft, John Stuart Mill, Betty Friedan, Millicent Fawcett

ideologies.name: Radical feminism
ideologies.oneLine: Patriarchy is the root of women's oppression, and it runs deep.
ideologies.believes: Male dominance is built into society, culture and private life, not just law. 'The personal is political': relationships, sexuality and housework are sites of power too. Real change means transforming society, not just reforming it.
ideologies.origins: Grew from the women's liberation movement of the late 1960s, especially in the United States.
ideologies.critics: Liberal feminists say it overstates the case and alienates potential allies. Intersectional feminists argue it can treat all women as having the same experience. Conservatives and many others reject its view of the family. It has also been divided internally over questions of sex and gender.
ideologies.thinkers: Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Andrea Dworkin, Catharine MacKinnon

ideologies.name: Socialist feminism
ideologies.oneLine: Women's oppression is tied to capitalism and unpaid work.
ideologies.believes: Sexism and economic exploitation reinforce each other. Women's unpaid domestic and caring labour keeps the economy running but is not valued. Freeing women means changing both gender roles and the economic system.
ideologies.origins: Combines Marxist analysis with feminism. It drew on Friedrich Engels' writing on the family and took shape in the 1970s.
ideologies.critics: Radical feminists say it reduces patriarchy to economics. Liberals and free-market thinkers dispute its critique of capitalism. Some Marxists have treated gender as secondary to class.
ideologies.thinkers: Alexandra Kollontai, Sheila Rowbotham, Silvia Federici, Nancy Fraser

ideologies.name: Black feminism and intersectionality
ideologies.oneLine: Race, gender and class overlap, so experiences of injustice differ.
ideologies.believes: A Black woman's experience is not just 'racism plus sexism' but its own thing. Movements focused on one form of inequality can miss people at the crossroads. Feminism should centre those most marginalised.
ideologies.origins: Rooted in nineteenth-century figures like Sojourner Truth, developed by the Combahee River Collective in 1977. The legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw coined 'intersectionality' in 1989.
ideologies.critics: Some critics argue it can encourage dividing people into ever smaller groups. Others say it is hard to apply in law and policy. Some on the left argue it shifts attention away from class.
ideologies.thinkers: Kimberlé Crenshaw, bell hooks, Audre Lorde, Patricia Hill Collins

ideologies.name: Nationalism
ideologies.oneLine: The nation is the basis of political community and self-government.
ideologies.believes: People who share a culture, language, history or territory form a nation and have a right to govern themselves. Loyalty to the nation is a source of meaning and solidarity. It comes in many forms: civic nationalism based on shared citizenship, and ethnic nationalism based on ancestry.
ideologies.origins: Spread after the French Revolution and through the 1800s, uniting Italy and Germany and later driving independence movements in Africa and Asia, including Ghana's in 1957.
ideologies.critics: Liberals and cosmopolitans say it divides humanity and can turn hostile to outsiders and minorities. Socialists say it hides class divisions. Its role in twentieth-century wars is a major warning. Defenders reply that it built democracy and freed colonies.
ideologies.thinkers: Johann Gottfried Herder, Giuseppe Mazzini, Kwame Nkrumah, Benedict Anderson (who studied it)

ideologies.name: Environmentalism
ideologies.oneLine: Human life depends on nature, and we must live within its limits.
ideologies.believes: Endless growth on a finite planet is not sustainable. Policy should protect ecosystems, cut pollution and tackle climate change. 'Light green' views seek reform within current systems; 'deep green' views argue nature has value in itself and society needs fundamental change.
ideologies.origins: Has roots in nineteenth-century conservation, but the modern movement grew from Rachel Carson's Silent Spring in 1962 and the first Earth Day in 1970.
ideologies.critics: Free-market critics say heavy regulation harms growth and the poorest. Some on the left say it can ignore workers and global inequality. Others argue that technology and innovation, not limits, are the answer.
ideologies.thinkers: Rachel Carson, Arne Næss, Wangari Maathai, E. F. Schumacher

ideologies.name: Anarchism
ideologies.oneLine: Society can and should organise itself without a state.
ideologies.believes: The state and other forced hierarchies are harmful and unnecessary. People can co-operate voluntarily through communities, unions and mutual aid. Left anarchists also oppose capitalism; anarcho-capitalists favour markets without a state.
ideologies.origins: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon first called himself an anarchist in 1840. It grew through the 1800s and was briefly put into practice in parts of Spain in the 1930s.
ideologies.critics: Most other traditions argue that without a state, the strong would dominate and order would collapse. Marxists say it lacks a realistic route to change. Critics point to few lasting examples.
ideologies.thinkers: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, Peter Kropotkin, Emma Goldman, Murray Bookchin

ideologies.name: Populism
ideologies.believes: Politics should express the will of ordinary people, which an out-of-touch establishment ignores. Most scholars see it as a style or 'thin' ideology that attaches to left or right ideas. Left populism targets economic elites; right populism often targets cultural elites and immigration.
ideologies.origins: The term comes from the American People's Party of the 1890s and Russian narodniks. It has risen across Europe and the Americas since the 2008 financial crisis.
ideologies.critics: Liberals warn it can undermine courts, the press and minority rights by claiming to speak for 'the' people. Others say it offers simple answers to complex problems. Defenders say it gives a voice to people mainstream politics has neglected.
ideologies.thinkers: Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe (left), Cas Mudde and Jan-Werner Müller (who study it)

ideologies.name: Christian democracy
ideologies.oneLine: Christian social values within a democratic, mixed economy.
ideologies.believes: Draws on Christian, especially Catholic, social teaching: human dignity, family, community and care for the poor. It supports markets but with a strong social safety net and co-operation between workers and employers. Decisions should be made at the most local level possible.
ideologies.origins: Grew from nineteenth-century Catholic social teaching and became a major force in post-war Western Europe, especially in Germany and Italy.
ideologies.critics: Secular liberals object to religion shaping politics. Free-market critics say it is too comfortable with state spending. Progressives say it is too conservative on social issues.
ideologies.thinkers: Konrad Adenauer, Jacques Maritain, Robert Schuman, Alcide De Gasperi

ideologies.name: Multiculturalism
ideologies.oneLine: Different cultures can and should live together with recognition and respect.
ideologies.believes: Cultural diversity is a strength, and minority groups should be able to keep their identity rather than fully assimilate. The state may recognise or support different cultures in public life.
ideologies.origins: Developed as policy in Canada in 1971 and spread to Britain, Australia and elsewhere as societies became more diverse after the Second World War.
ideologies.critics: Conservatives and some liberals say it can weaken shared national identity and integration. Some feminists worry it can protect practices harmful to women. Some on the left say it focuses on culture rather than economic inequality.
ideologies.thinkers: Charles Taylor, Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, Tariq Modood
